seoTitle: How to Add Custom HTML Code to Elementor in WordPress
metaDescription: Embed custom HTML, scripts, and widgets in Elementor using the built-in HTML widget. This guide covers safe code placement and styling with CSS.
intro: Elementor's HTML widget is the quiet workaround that lets you drop in custom code, embed a third-party widget, or fire off a script without touching a single theme file. It's the same widget whether you're on Elementor Free or Pro, which makes it one of the more reliable tools in the page builder. This guide walks through opening the editor, finding the widget, pasting in real code, and checking the result before you publish — the exact sequence that trips people up the first time they try it.

steps.heading: Open Elementor from your WordPress dashboard
steps.body: Log into wp-admin and click Elementor in the left sidebar to land on its home screen, where you'll see a Create a Page button alongside prompts for building with AI or starting from a template. This screen isn't where you'll paste any code — it's just the entry point — but it's worth knowing it exists separately from the classic WordPress Pages list, since Elementor keeps its own dashboard for templates, settings, and add-ons. If you're adding HTML to a page that already exists rather than a new one, you can skip past this screen entirely and jump straight to your Pages list.

image.caption: The Elementor home screen inside WordPress, reached from the Elementor item in the admin sidebar.

steps.heading: Find your page and launch the editor
steps.body: Go to Pages in the WordPress sidebar, hover over the page you want to edit, and click Edit with Elementor rather than the standard Edit link — the standard editor won't give you access to Elementor's widgets. This distinction matters more than it sounds like it should: a lot of people end up in the block editor wondering where the HTML widget went, when they simply launched the wrong editor. Once you click through, Elementor loads the page in its drag-and-drop canvas with the widget panel docked on the left.

image.caption: The WordPress Pages list, with Edit with Elementor as the link that opens the page in the Elementor canvas rather than the default editor.

steps.heading: Add the HTML widget to your layout
steps.body: In the widget panel, search "HTML" and you'll see the HTML widget appear — it's part of the free widget set, so no Pro upgrade is required. Drag it onto the section or container where you want the code to render, the same way you'd place a heading or image widget. Elementor treats it like any other element: it can sit inside a column, stack above or below other widgets, and be resized or repositioned afterward without affecting the code inside it.

steps.heading: Paste your custom HTML code
steps.body: Once the widget is placed, its settings panel opens on the left with a Content tab showing an HTML Code field — a plain text editor where you type or paste your markup directly. This is where an embed snippet from a third-party service, a custom form, or a hand-written HTML block goes; Elementor renders it live in the canvas as you type, so you can see roughly how it will look before saving. There's no visual formatting toolbar here on purpose — it's a raw code field, which is exactly what makes it flexible enough to hold scripts and embeds that a normal text widget would strip out.

image.caption: The Edit HTML panel with its HTML Code field, open on a fresh container ready for a pasted code snippet.

steps.heading: Apply CSS or JS if the embed needs styling
steps.body: Plenty of embedded widgets and scripts come with their own styling and don't need anything extra, but if your snippet looks unstyled or misaligned, Elementor gives you two ways to fix it. Custom CSS can be added per-element in the widget's Advanced tab, or site-wide under Elementor's Custom Code settings if the styling needs to apply everywhere. JavaScript can go directly inside the HTML widget's code field wrapped in script tags, or in Custom Code if you want it to load on every page rather than just this one section.

steps.heading: Save and preview before publishing
steps.body: Click Update (or Publish, on a new page) and then use Elementor's preview icon to check the live page rather than trusting the editor canvas alone — some scripts and embeds only behave correctly outside the builder's iframe. Check both desktop and the mobile preview toggle at the top of the editor, since an HTML embed that fits cleanly on a wide screen can overflow or get clipped on mobile. If something looks broken, it's almost always a missing closing tag or a script that needs to load after the page rather than during it.

faq.question: Do I need Elementor Pro to add HTML code to my page?
faq.answer: No, the HTML widget is available in both Elementor Free and Elementor Pro, so you don't need the paid version just to embed custom code.

faq.question: Can adding custom HTML break my WordPress site?
faq.answer: Poorly formatted or conflicting code can cause display issues, so it's worth previewing changes — including on mobile — before publishing and undoing anything that looks off.

faq.question: Can I add JavaScript through the Elementor HTML widget, not just HTML?
faq.answer: Yes, the HTML widget accepts script tags along with HTML, so you can embed JavaScript-driven widgets or custom functionality the same way.

faq.question: Will custom HTML added through Elementor work with any WordPress theme?
faq.answer: Yes, since the HTML widget renders independently of the theme's templates, it should work consistently across different WordPress themes.

faq.question: Why don't I see the HTML widget option in my editor?
faq.answer: Make sure you opened the page with Edit with Elementor rather than the default WordPress editor — the HTML widget only appears inside Elementor's own widget panel.
